title: Huntington’s Disease in the Era of Single-Cell and Single-Nucleus Transcriptomics: Complementarity with Bulk RNA-seq and Findings at Cellular Resolution
content: Huntington’s disease (HD) is an example of selective neuronal vulnerability. An expansion of the CAG trinucleotide repeat in the huntingtin gene (HTT), present in every cell of the body, drives an early and hierarchical degeneration of the striatal spiny projection neurons (SPNs), predominantly those of the indirect pathway and the striosomal compartment. For two decades, microarrays and bulk tissue RNA sequencing (bulk RNA-seq) defined the regional transcriptional signatures of the disease, but by averaging heterogeneous cell populations they could not assign these changes to defined cell types or separate the net loss of neurons from the dysregulation of the surviving cells. Single-nucleus transcriptomics (snRNA-seq) addressed this limit by providing cellular resolution. With it, the vulnerability of the SPNs was dissected into the collapse of the striosome-matrix axis,  more vulnerable subpopulations, and the loss of neuronal identity through bidirectional dysregulation. Glial states that whole-tissue analysis could not separate were also resolved,  among them a compensatory astrocytic state and an oligodendroglial maturation deficit, together with neuroimmune mechanisms such as neuronal innate immunity and the  recruitment of cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Coupling the transcriptome with per-cell CAG measurement supports a model in which somatic expansion becomes toxic to the neuron only once it crosses a critical threshold, which places it as a temporal determinant of neurodegeneration in the striatal spiny projection neurons. Far from replacing bulk approaches, cellular resolution complements them, because it allows whole-tissue cohorts to be reinterpreted through deconvolution. This review synthesizes these findings and identifies which of them depended on cellular resolution.
